notes.front: What is Assured Workloads?
notes.back: A service for configuring a sovereign data and access boundary, with residency, access and personnel controls, for sensitive workloads.
notes.explanation: It simplifies regulated workloads by applying predefined control packages to folders.
notes.example: Like a bonded warehouse inside a commercial port: the same cranes and roads, but stricter rules on who enters and what leaves.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Overview of Assured Workloads”, “Overview of Assured Workloads”
notes.evidence: Assured Workloads enables organizations in the private and public sectors to configure a sovereign data and access boundary with residency, access, and personnel controls for sensitive workloads in the cloud. You can use Assured Workloads to simplify management and configuration of regulated workloads by applying predefined control packages to folders.

notes.front: In Assured Workloads, what is a control package?
notes.back: A predefined set of controls that forms the foundation for compliance enforcement in Assured Workloads.
notes.explanation: Packages exist for regional data boundaries, regulatory data boundaries and Sovereign Controls by Partners.
notes.example: Like choosing a building-regulations pack for a hospital wing, which then applies to every room built inside it.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Overview of Assured Workloads”, “Control packages”
notes.evidence: Control packages are the foundation for compliance enforcement for Assured Workloads. Assured Workloads control packages are available for the following control types: regional data boundaries, regulatory data boundaries, and Sovereign Controls by Partners.

notes.front: What does data residency describe?
notes.back: Where your data is stored at rest.
notes.explanation: Google Cloud lets you control that location to help you comply with residency requirements.
notes.example: A regulator requires that a bank’s customer records stay on storage inside its home country.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Data residency”, “Data residency”
notes.evidence: Data residency describes where your data is stored at rest. To help comply with data residency requirements, Google Cloud gives you the ability to control where that data is stored.

notes.front: What does an Assured Workloads data boundary let you do?
notes.back: Specify a Google Cloud region where your data must reside, preventing data storage outside that region.
notes.explanation: Some data boundaries also give you independent control over Google’s access to your data.
notes.example: Like a rule that a firm’s paper archive may only be kept in warehouses within one country.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Overview of Assured Workloads”, “Regional data boundaries”
notes.evidence: Some data boundaries also let you exercise independent control over Google's access to your data, such as by approving access only for specific provider behaviors that you deem appropriate and necessary. These data boundaries let you specify a Google Cloud region where your data must reside and prevents data storage outside of that region.

notes.front: What are Sovereign Controls by Partners in Assured Workloads?
notes.back: Control packages operated and managed by partners, letting a local trusted partner manage encryption keys, access justification and audits.
notes.explanation: These packages also help enforce data residency.
notes.example: Like appointing a local notary to hold the spare keys and sign off every visit to your premises.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Overview of Assured Workloads”, “Sovereign Controls by Partners”
notes.evidence: Assured Workloads also offers control packages that are operated and managed by partners through Sovereign Controls by Partners. Sovereign Controls by Partners lets you use a local, trusted partner to manage encryption keys, access justification, and audits. These control packages help enforce data residency

notes.front: What do Access Transparency logs record?
notes.back: The actions that Google personnel take when accessing Customer Data.
notes.explanation: Each entry gives the affected resource and action, the time, the reason and information about the accessor.
notes.example: Like a landlord’s entry book that records each time maintenance staff let themselves into your flat, and why.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Overview of Access Transparency”, “Overview”
notes.evidence: Access Transparency logs record the actions that Google personnel take when accessing Customer Data. Access Transparency log entries include details such as the affected resource and action, the time of the action, the reason for the action, and information about the accessor.

notes.front: What is the Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS)?
notes.back: An information security standard for businesses that handle credit and debit card information, created by the PCI Security Standards Council.
notes.explanation: The council that created it includes every major payment card company.
notes.example: An online bike shop that takes card payments on its own checkout page.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “PCI Data Security Standard compliance”, “PCI Data Security Standard compliance”
notes.evidence: The PCI Data Security Standard, created by the PCI Security Standards Council, is an information security standard for businesses that handle payment card (both credit and debit) information. The PCI Security Standards Council includes every major payment card company.
introduces: Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard
uses: Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard

notes.front: What is the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA)?
notes.back: A 1996 United States federal law setting privacy and security rules for organisations that must safeguard individuals’ protected health information.
notes.explanation: The organisations it binds are called covered entities or business associates.
notes.example: A chain of physiotherapy clinics that keeps patients’ treatment notes in a cloud database.
notes.source: Google Cloud website, “HIPAA”, “HIPAA”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
introduces: Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act
uses: Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act

notes.front: What is the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA)?
notes.back: A 1998 United States rule governing the online collection of personal information from children under 13.
notes.explanation: It applies to operators of sites or services aimed at under-13s, and to others that knowingly collect such information from them.
notes.example: A phonics app for six-year-olds that asks for a child’s first name and a contact email.
notes.source: Google Cloud website, “COPPA (U.S.)”, “COPPA (U.S.)”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a SOC 2 report?
notes.back: An independent auditor’s report on a service organisation’s controls against criteria such as security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality or privacy.
notes.explanation: Customers use it to judge the risks of relying on the audited systems over the period it covers.
notes.example: A bank’s supplier-risk team asks its cloud provider for the latest report before renewing a contract.
notes.source: Google Cloud website, “SOC 2”, “SOC 2”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is Compliance Reports Manager?
notes.back: Google Cloud’s place for on-demand access to compliance resources such as certificates, SOC 2 reports and self-assessments, at no extra cost.
notes.explanation: Some items need a sign-in, and confidential ones may not be passed outside your organisation without permission.
notes.example: An internal auditor preparing the annual review downloads the provider’s newest audit report there.
notes.source: Google Cloud website, “Compliance Reports Manager”, “Compliance Reports Manager”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is personally identifiable information (PII)?
notes.back: Direct and indirect identifiers of people that should not be exposed in plain text, such as in shared analytical datasets.
notes.explanation: Sensitive Data Protection can transform such identifiers, for example by pseudonymisation, date shifting or bucketing.
notes.example: A support ticket in which a customer typed their home address and date of birth.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Sensitive Data Protection overview”, “When to use Sensitive Data Protection”
notes.evidence: De-identify analytical datasets while preserving utility: Transform direct and indirect identifiers using pseudonymization, date shifting, or bucketing so research and business intelligence teams can analyze data without exposing plaintext PII.

notes.front: Which products does the Well-Architected Framework name for meeting regulatory, compliance and privacy needs?
notes.back: Assured Workloads, the Organization Policy Service and the compliance resource center.
notes.explanation: The principle asks you to adhere to industry regulations, compliance standards and privacy requirements.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Well-Architected Framework: Security, privacy, and compliance pillar”, “Core principles”
notes.evidence: Meet regulatory, compliance, and privacy needs: Adhere to industry-specific regulations, compliance standards, and privacy requirements. Google Cloud helps you meet these obligations through products like Assured Workloads, Organization Policy Service, and our compliance resource center.

notes.front: A health-data company must keep all data in European Union regions and limit which Google support staff can access it, applied automatically to a group of projects. What fits?
notes.back: C: An Assured Workloads folder with a suitable data-boundary control package
notes.choices:
A) A service perimeter around the projects
B) Labels on every resource naming the allowed region
C) An Assured Workloads folder with a suitable data-boundary control package
D) Regional secrets in Secret Manager
notes.choicesExplained: A controls data movement between services, not storage location or support staff. B records intent but enforces nothing. D covers secrets only.
notes.explanation: Assured Workloads suits organisations that must store data in certain regions and control Google personnel access.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Overview of Assured Workloads”, “Use cases for Assured Workloads”
notes.evidence: Organizations that must store their data within certain regions or countries. Organizations that must control Google Cloud personnel access to their data.

notes.front: How are the controls in an Assured Workloads control package enforced?
notes.back: Through organisation policy constraints and other features.
notes.explanation: Which Google Cloud products are supported varies by control package.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Overview of Assured Workloads”, “Control packages”
notes.evidence: These controls are enforced using organization policy constraints and other features. Support for Google Cloud products and services varies by control package.

notes.front: Which type of control package supports data residency by restricting the geographic location where resources can be stored?
notes.back: Regional data boundaries.
notes.explanation: For example, the European Union data boundary package limits resource usage to European Union regions only.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Overview of Assured Workloads”, “Regional data boundaries”
notes.evidence: These data boundaries let you specify a Google Cloud region where your data must reside and prevents data storage outside of that region. For example, if the EU Data Boundary control package is applied, data residency controls are implemented to restrict resource usage to EU-only regions.

notes.front: Which type of control package deploys a set of controls for a specific regulatory or compliance requirement?
notes.back: Regulatory data boundaries.
notes.explanation: Examples include packages for FedRAMP Moderate and High, and for Criminal Justice Information Systems.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Overview of Assured Workloads”, “Regulatory data boundaries”
notes.evidence: Regulatory data boundary control packages let you deploy a set of controls to address a specific regulatory or compliance requirement. Google Cloud includes regulatory data boundaries for the following: Canada Controlled Goods Program (CGP) Criminal Justice Information Systems (CJIS) FedRAMP Moderate and FedRAMP High

notes.front: A defence supplier must meet the International Traffic in Arms Regulations on Google Cloud, with keys kept apart from the workloads for separation of duties. What fits?
notes.back: C: The regulatory data boundary for those regulations, which requires CMEKs in a separate key project
notes.choices:
A) A regional data boundary with Google default encryption
B) Organisation policies written by hand, with no Assured Workloads folder
C) The regulatory data boundary for those regulations, which requires CMEKs in a separate key project
D) Customer-supplied encryption keys in each workload project
notes.choicesExplained: A lacks the regulation’s controls and customer-managed keys. B misses the packaged controls and violation monitoring. D keeps keys beside the workloads, and CSEKs are limited to two services.
notes.explanation: That package requires customer-managed keys and uses a key management project separate from other resources.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Overview of Assured Workloads”, “Key management”
notes.evidence: For example, the Data Boundary for ITAR control package requires the use of customer-managed encryption keys (CMEKs). To enable separation of duties, the Data Boundary for ITAR control package uses a key management project that is separate from other deployed resources and creates a unique key ring for storage within a compliance location.

notes.front: Access Approval versus Access Transparency: what does each give you?
notes.back: Access Approval: you authorise Google personnel’s requests to access Customer Data. Access Transparency: you learn when Customer Data was accessed.
notes.explanation: One is a gate before access, the other a record after it.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Overview of Access Transparency”, “Overview of Access Transparency”
notes.evidence: Access Approval lets you authorize requests from Google personnel to access Customer Data, and Access Transparency helps you discover information about when Customer Data is accessed.

notes.front: Cloud Audit Logs versus Access Transparency logs: whose actions does each record?
notes.back: Cloud Audit Logs: members of your Google Cloud organisation. Access Transparency: Google personnel.
notes.explanation: Used together they give audit logging of both customer actions and Google administrative access.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Overview of Access Transparency”, “Overview”
notes.evidence: Cloud Audit Logs records the actions that members of your Google Cloud organization have taken in your Google Cloud resources, whereas Access Transparency logs record the actions taken by Google personnel. When used together, Cloud Audit Logs and Access Transparency logs provide you audit logging on both customer actions and Google administrative access to Customer Data.

notes.front: An insurer’s regulator wants evidence that cloud provider staff touch its data only for valid reasons such as support cases, fed into its security monitoring tool. What fits?
notes.back: B: Access Transparency logs
notes.choices:
A) Data Access audit logs
B) Access Transparency logs
C) Security Command Center findings
D) Organisation policy dry-run logs
notes.choicesExplained: A records access by your own principals, not Google staff. C reports threats and misconfigurations. D shows policy violations, not provider access.
notes.explanation: Verifying that Google personnel access data only for valid business reasons is a stated use of Access Transparency.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Overview of Access Transparency”, “When to use Access Transparency”
notes.evidence: Verifying that Google personnel are accessing your content only for valid business reasons, such as fixing an outage or attending to your support requests.

notes.front: Which organisation policy constraint restricts where new in-scope resources can be created?
notes.back: The Resource Locations constraint.
notes.explanation: It can be set at the organisation, folder or project level of the resource hierarchy.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Data residency”, “Assured Workloads and data residency”
notes.evidence: Organizations with data residency requirements can set up a Resource Locations organization policy constraint that restricts the location of new in-scope resources at the organization, project, or folder level of their resource hierarchy.

notes.front: Do Google’s data residency commitments cover resource identifiers, attributes and labels?
notes.back: No; they apply to Customer Data at rest, which excludes resource identifiers, attributes and other data labels.
notes.explanation: Names and labels you give resources may therefore sit outside the chosen location.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Data residency”, “Note on Customer Data and Service Data”
notes.evidence: our data residency commitments apply to Customer Data at rest for services that can be configured for data location. As noted there, "Customer Data does not include resource identifiers, attributes, or other data labels."

notes.front: A company must ensure new resources in its analytics folder are created only in Canadian regions, and it cannot yet adopt Assured Workloads. What should it set?
notes.back: C: A Resource Locations organisation policy on the folder
notes.choices:
A) A service perimeter around the analytics folder
B) A label on the folder reading “Canada only”
C) A Resource Locations organisation policy on the folder
D) Data Access audit logs, reviewed monthly
notes.choicesExplained: A limits data movement between services, not where resources are created. B enforces nothing. D detects problems after the fact.
notes.explanation: The constraint restricts the location of new in-scope resources at the level where it is set.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Data residency”, “Assured Workloads and data residency”
notes.evidence: Organizations with data residency requirements can set up a Resource Locations organization policy constraint that restricts the location of new in-scope resources at the organization, project, or folder level of their resource hierarchy.

notes.front: In PCI DSS terms, what is the cardholder data environment?
notes.back: Any part of your app that holds or transfers cardholder data, including the account number or card-related PII.
notes.explanation: Card-related personal information counts, not only the card number itself.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “PCI Data Security Standard compliance”, “Definitions”
notes.evidence: CDE: Acronym for cardholder data environment. This acronym refers to any part of your app that holds or transfers any cardholder data, including the payment account number or any personally identifiable information related to the card.

notes.front: How does Google’s PCI DSS guide recommend separating the payment-processing environment?
notes.back: Fully isolate it from standard production and from development and quality-assurance environments, using a separate Google Cloud account.
notes.explanation: Isolation simplifies access restriction and compliance auditing.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “PCI Data Security Standard compliance”, “Setting up a new account”
notes.evidence: To simplify access restriction and compliance auditing, create a production-quality, payment-processing environment that is fully isolated from your standard production environment and any dev and QA environments (requirement 6.5.3). To ensure isolation, create and use a Google Cloud account that is separate from your core production environment account.

notes.front: A retailer’s payment service shares projects with its catalogue, reviews and test systems, so auditors treat everything as in scope. What does Google’s PCI DSS guide recommend?
notes.back: D: Isolate payment processing in its own account or projects
notes.choices:
A) Encrypt the catalogue database with customer-managed keys
B) Give every developer the Owner basic role to speed up fixes
C) Move all systems into one larger project
D) Isolate payment processing in its own account or projects
notes.choicesExplained: A changes key control but not what is in scope. B breaks least privilege. C mixes in-scope and other work even further.
notes.explanation: Separate projects for in-scope work give isolation equivalent to a separate account.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “PCI Data Security Standard compliance”, “Setting up a new account”
notes.evidence: Users experienced with Identity and Access Management (IAM) configuration can accomplish equivalent isolation by using separate projects for in-scope work.

notes.front: Does Google Cloud’s PCI DSS compliance cover the operating system packages and apps you deploy?
notes.back: No; complying for the operating system packages and apps you deploy is your responsibility.
notes.explanation: Google doesn’t control security for the software that merchants deploy on Google Cloud.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “PCI Data Security Standard compliance”, “Committed to compliance”
notes.evidence: Google doesn't control security for the operating system, packages, or apps that merchants deploy on Google Cloud. It is your responsibility to comply with PCI DSS requirements for operating system packages and apps that you deploy, in addition to other customizations required by your architecture.

notes.front: Why can Google Cloud support a merchant’s PCI DSS needs whatever its merchant level?
notes.back: Google Cloud is a Level 1 PCI DSS 4.0–compliant service provider.
notes.explanation: The provider side is therefore covered whether the merchant is small or at the highest level.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “PCI Data Security Standard compliance”, “Background”
notes.evidence: Because Google Cloud is a Level 1 PCI DSS 4.0–compliant service provider, it can support your PCI DSS compliance needs no matter what your company's merchant level is.

notes.front: Does Google’s automatic encryption at rest meet the PCI DSS rule that stored primary account numbers be secured?
notes.back: Not on its own: Google doesn’t automatically perform the one-way hashing, truncation or tokenisation the rules also require.
notes.explanation: Requirement 3.5 asks for the account number to be secured wherever it is stored.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “PCI Data Security Standard compliance”, “Cloud Storage”
notes.evidence: Requirement 3.5 stipulates that a primary account number (PAN) is secured wherever it is stored. While Google automatically offers encryption at rest, it doesn't automatically perform the one-way hashes, truncation, or tokenization that the rules also require.

notes.front: Which PCI DSS self-assessment questionnaire type fits a merchant that has fully outsourced card processing, so it never touches card data?
notes.back: Type A.
notes.explanation: Customers leave the merchant’s domain to pay, then return to the app.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “PCI Data Security Standard compliance”, “Background”
notes.evidence: A Merchants that have fully outsourced payment card processing to a third-party site. Customers leave your domain (including through an <iframe> web form), complete payment, and then return to your app. In other words, your company can't touch customer card data in any way.

notes.front: Which PCI DSS self-assessment questionnaire type fits a merchant whose own servers call a payment processor’s interface, even with tokenisation?
notes.back: Type D.
notes.explanation: Any online merchant that does not qualify for the two lighter types falls into type D.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “PCI Data Security Standard compliance”, “Background”
notes.evidence: D Merchants that accept payments online and don't qualify for SAQ A or SAQ A-EP. This type includes all merchants that call a payment processor API from their own servers, regardless of tokenization.

notes.front: Before using Google Cloud with protected health information, what must a customer that is subject to HIPAA do?
notes.back: Review and accept Google’s Business Associate Agreement.
notes.explanation: That agreement governs how Google processes the health information; customers arrange it through their account managers.
notes.source: Google Cloud website, “HIPAA”, “HIPAA”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A hospital group has accepted Google’s Business Associate Agreement and now assumes its cloud system is HIPAA compliant. What is accurate?
notes.back: C: Not yet: it must build a compliant solution on covered services and implement the controls
notes.choices:
A) Yes, as long as the data stays in one region
B) Yes: the agreement transfers compliance to Google
C) Not yet: it must build a compliant solution on covered services and implement the controls
D) No: the agreement must first be rewritten to the group’s own terms
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: the covered entity stays responsible. A invents a condition: the agreement covers all regions, but that alone does not make a solution compliant. D is wrong: the agreement cannot be modified.
notes.explanation: Signing the agreement is a prerequisite, not the finished job.
notes.source: Google Cloud website, “HIPAA”, “HIPAA”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Under COPPA, what does Google contractually require of schools that use Google Workspace for Education?
notes.back: That they meet COPPA’s parental consent requirements.
notes.explanation: With consent in place, the education core services can be used in line with the law.
notes.source: Google Cloud website, “COPPA (U.S.)”, “COPPA (U.S.)”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A start-up launches a spelling-game website aimed at eight-year-olds that collects players’ email addresses. Which rule most directly governs that collection?
notes.back: D: COPPA
notes.choices:
A) HIPAA
B) PCI DSS
C) SOC 2
D) COPPA
notes.choicesExplained: A covers protected health information. B covers payment card data. C is an audit report on a provider’s controls, not a law about users.
notes.explanation: COPPA covers operators of online services aimed at children under 13 that collect their personal information.
notes.source: Google Cloud website, “COPPA (U.S.)”, “COPPA (U.S.)”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: SOC 2 Type I versus Type II: what does each report cover?
notes.back: Type I: control design at one point in time. Type II: design and operating effectiveness over a period. Google Cloud issues only Type II.
notes.explanation: A Type II report shows the controls actually worked throughout the period, not just that they were designed.
notes.source: Google Cloud website, “SOC 2”, “SOC 2”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: From a security point of view, what does centralising log storage give you?
notes.back: One storage location, which can simplify the work of security analysts.
notes.explanation: It also gives a single place to query when searching for trends or investigating issues.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Route log entries”, “Examples: Centralize your log storage”
notes.evidence: Centralized storage provides a single place to query for log data, which simplifies your queries when you are searching for trends or investigating issues. From a security perspective, you also have one storage location, which can simplify the tasks of your security analysts.

notes.front: If you centralise log storage in one project, what can protect that project from accidental deletion?
notes.back: A lien on the project.
notes.explanation: Centralising places all the log data in one project, so that project is worth protecting.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Route log entries”, “Examples: Centralize your log storage”
notes.evidence: If you centralize your log storage, then consider whether to place a lien on the project that stores your log data. A lien can prevent the accidental deletion of a project.

notes.front: Auditors want every project’s logs in a folder kept in one place that analysts can query, safe from someone deleting the storage project by mistake. What fits?
notes.back: A: Route the folder’s logs into one central project and place a lien on it
notes.choices:
A) Route the folder’s logs into one central project and place a lien on it
B) Leave logs in each project and grant auditors access to all of them
C) Export logs weekly to laptops for review
D) Turn off Data Access audit logs to cut volume
notes.choicesExplained: B keeps logs scattered and gives no deletion protection. C takes records out of controlled storage. D removes evidence auditors may need.
notes.explanation: Centralised storage gives one place to query, and a lien can prevent accidental deletion of the project.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Route log entries”, “Centralize log storage for projects in a folder”
notes.evidence: In your folder, you create a project named CentralStorage. Create an intercepting aggregated sink for your folder and you configure it to route all log entries. You set the destination of the sink to be the project named CentralStorage.
